q: Allocation of overheads means:

options.A: Splitting a common expense among cost centres on a suitable basis
options.B: Charging an overhead wholly to one cost centre that can be directly identified
options.C: Charging overheads to jobs at a predetermined rate
options.D: Writing off overheads to the costing profit and loss account

q: Apportionment of overheads is needed when:

options.A: A cost can be traced directly to one job
options.B: Overheads are absorbed at a predetermined rate
options.C: A cost centre performs services for another
options.D: An overhead is common to two or more cost centres and must be shared

q: Absorption of overheads means:

options.A: Charging overheads to individual jobs or work orders by a rate
options.C: Assigning a cost wholly to one cost centre
options.D: Carrying unabsorbed overheads to the next year

q: The main difference between allocation and apportionment is that:

options.A: Allocation uses rates while apportionment uses actuals
options.B: Allocation is for direct costs and apportionment for indirect costs
options.C: Allocation charges the whole amount to one centre; apportionment splits common costs on a basis
options.D: Allocation is done monthly while apportionment is annual

q: Which of the following is an example of an allocated overhead?

options.A: Factory rent shared by several shops
options.B: Salary of a foreman supervising only the wheel shop
options.D: Canteen expenses of the whole workshop

q: Which overhead would normally be apportioned?

options.A: Building rent used by several shops
options.B: Wages of a machine operator in the foundry
options.C: Salary of the wheel shop supervisor
options.D: Depreciation of a lathe used in one shop

q: Overhead absorbed by a job is calculated by:

options.A: Adding actual overheads to the job cost
options.B: Dividing total overheads by the number of jobs
options.C: Charging actual indirect costs to the job
options.D: Applying a predetermined rate per unit of base to the job

q: Primary apportionment of overheads results in:

options.B: Final cost of each work order
options.C: Departmental overhead totals before service department re-apportionment
options.D: The balance carried to the next year

q: Building rent is usually apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.B: Floor area occupied by each shop

q: Power cost is best apportioned to shops on the basis of:
Supervision costs are generally apportioned on the basis of:

options.D: Number of workers in each shop

q: Depreciation of plant is apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.C: Value of machinery in each shop

q: Canteen and welfare expenses are apportioned on the basis of:

options.A: Number of employees in each department

q: Insurance of factory buildings is apportioned on the basis of:
The works manager's salary is apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.D: Direct labour hours of each shop

q: A suitable basis of apportionment should:

options.A: Be the same for every overhead
options.C: Bear an equitable relation to the benefit each centre receives

q: Which of these is a service department in a railway workshop?
Service department costs are ultimately charged to:

options.B: The costing profit and loss account directly

q: Service department costs are re-apportioned because:

options.B: They render no direct saleable output, so production must bear them
options.C: They are too small to matter

q: Plant maintenance costs are apportioned to production shops on the basis of:

options.D: Maintenance hours worked for each shop

q: Tool room expenses are re-apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.A: Direct labour hours or value of tools issued

q: Workshop transport costs are apportioned on the basis of:

options.C: Weight or tonne-kilometres of material carried for each shop

q: Re-apportionment means:

options.A: Dividing common overheads among all departments
options.B: Redistributing service department costs to production departments

q: In the step-down method of re-apportionment:

options.A: All service departments are closed simultaneously
options.B: Mutual services between service departments are fully recognised
options.C: Only production departments receive the costs
options.D: Service departments are closed in sequence and receive no further charge once closed

q: The reciprocal method of re-apportionment:

options.A: Recognises services rendered mutually between service departments
options.C: Closes service departments in alphabetical order
options.D: Uses only one basis for all departments

q: Under the step-down method, the first service department to be closed is:

options.A: The one with the highest cost
options.C: The one serving the greatest number of other service departments

q: In repeated distribution, the process continues until:

options.B: Balances left in service departments become negligible

q: The direct method of re-apportionment:

options.A: Ignores services between service departments entirely

q: Shop on-cost comprises:

options.C: Indirect expenses of a particular shop, such as supervision and consumables

e: Shop on-cost comprises the indirect expenses incurred within a particular shop, as distinct from general on-cost, which is common to the workshop as a whole.

q: General on-cost comprises:

options.B: Workshop-level overheads like managerial establishment and general office
options.D: Cost of tools issued to a shop

e: General on-cost comprises indirect expenses common to the workshop as a whole, such as general administration and supervision, apportioned among the shops.

q: A job worked in a shop bears:

options.D: Both the shop on-cost of its shop and a share of general on-cost

q: The difference between shop on-cost and general on-cost is that:

options.A: Shop on-cost is shop-specific while general on-cost relates to the whole workshop
options.B: Shop on-cost is direct and general on-cost is indirect
options.C: Shop on-cost is fixed and general on-cost is variable

q: Shop on-cost rate is normally expressed as:

options.B: A percentage of the shop's direct labour

q: General on-cost rate is normally expressed as:

options.C: A percentage of the total direct labour of the workshop

A predetermined overhead rate is based on:

options.A: Budgeted overheads divided by the budgeted base
options.B: Actual overheads divided by actual output
options.D: A rate fixed by the Railway Board

q: Predetermined overhead rates are used so that:

options.A: Actual costs are always recovered exactly
options.C: Rates remain unchanged for ten years
options.D: Jobs can be costed promptly without waiting for actuals

q: The predetermined on-cost rate is computed as:

options.A: Actual overheads divided by actual direct wages
options.B: Estimated overheads divided by the estimated base such as direct labour hours
options.C: Total cost divided by number of jobs
options.D: Prime cost plus a fixed margin

q: An actual overhead rate can be computed only:

options.C: After the period ends, from actual overheads and the actual base

q: A blanket overhead rate means:

options.A: One rate for the whole workshop applied to all jobs
options.B: A rate that covers only one shop
options.D: A rate based on material cost

q: Departmental overhead rates are preferred when:

options.B: Shops differ in mechanisation or overhead intensity

q: Over-absorption of overheads occurs when:

options.B: Fewer jobs are completed than planned
options.C: Overheads absorbed by jobs exceed actual overheads incurred

q: Under-absorption of overheads occurs when:

options.A: Actual overheads exceed the overheads charged to jobs
options.B: More jobs are completed than planned
options.C: Actual overheads are lower than budgeted

q: Under-absorption usually results from:

options.D: Lower activity than estimated or higher actual overheads

q: A small under or over absorption at year-end is:

options.B: Written off to the costing profit and loss account
options.C: Added to the next year's rate

q: A large abnormal under-absorption should be:

options.D: Treated as an abnormal loss and not loaded on to jobs

q: The proforma on-cost account shows a credit balance when:

options.B: Actual and absorbed on-cost are equal

q: Year-end clearance of on-cost differences ensures that:

options.A: Jobs carry only normal overheads while abnormal differences go to profit and loss
options.C: Next year's rate is always higher

q: The on-cost rate as a percentage of direct labour is:

options.A: Direct labour divided by overheads, times 100
options.B: Overheads divided by direct labour, times 100
options.D: Prime cost divided by overheads, times 100

q: Railway workshops use direct labour as the on-cost base mainly because:

options.A: Workshops are labour-intensive and labour records are readily available
options.C: The Railway Board forbids other bases

If direct labour rises while overheads stay unchanged, the on-cost percentage:
Fixed overheads are those which:

options.A: Remain constant in total within the relevant range of output
options.B: Vary directly with every unit produced

q: Variable overheads:

options.C: Vary in direct proportion to the level of activity

q: Under absorption costing, fixed overheads are:

options.A: Written off wholly to the profit and loss account
options.B: Absorbed into job costs like other overheads

q: A departmental overhead rate means:

options.A: One rate for the entire workshop
options.B: A rate based on material cost
options.C: A rate fixed for all India
options.D: A separate on-cost rate computed for each shop or department

q: The main advantage of departmental on-cost rates is:

options.B: More equitable charging where departments differ in conditions

q: Power house costs are apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.C: Metered kilowatt-hours consumed by each shop

q: Plant maintenance costs are apportioned to shops on the basis of:

options.A: Maintenance hours spent on each shop's plant

q: Where meters are absent, power cost may be apportioned on:

options.D: Machine hours or installed horsepower multiplied by hours run
